description: The elevator is stealing your strength in ten-second rides. Take the floors-until-it-burns test, watch what daily stairs do across week one, week two and week four, and learn why taking the stairs is a strength habit hiding inside your commute.

scenes.narration: Here is your test. Find the tallest staircase you can, at work, at the station, anywhere. Start climbing at one steady pace, no racing, no stopping. Count the floors. The moment your legs burn so hard you have to slow down or grab the rail, stop. That floor is your number. Most people are shocked how small it is. Keep it written down, because taking the stairs every day is about to move that floor higher than you expect, and at the end I will tell you exactly what your floor says about your leg power.

scenes.label: BEFORE THE BURN IS THE LINE
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Three floors at a steady pace, no rail, no slowdown, is where ordinary legs end and trained legs begin. Under two floors, the burn wins fast, and that just means climbing is a stranger to your legs. Over six, you climb like the building is a hill you own. Your floor today is not a grade. It is a starting altitude, and this habit raises it.
scenes.sub: under 2: the burn wins early - over 6: hill legs

scenes.narration: Week one is about the decision, not the burn. You take the stairs when the elevator is right there, and it feels like a small daily argument with yourself. By day seven the argument ends. The stairs become the default, and something physical follows: the burn that used to arrive on floor two now waits until floor three. Your legs did not grow in a week. They learned the route, and a learned route costs less every single time you climb it.

Week two, you stop noticing the climb. Week four, you test again, and the burn that owned floor two now shows up on floor four, sometimes five. Multiply that by a month of commutes and the math is quiet but huge: hundreds of single-leg presses you never scheduled, never drove to a gym for, never recovered from. The building became your training partner. That is what happens when the habit carries the load: the power arrives as a side effect of how you live.

lines: Climbing loads one leg at a time.
beats.title: EVERY FLOOR IS REPS

scenes.narration: The mechanism is simple physics. Level walking shares the work between two legs and momentum. Climbing does not. Each step parks your full bodyweight on one leg and asks the glute and thigh to lift it straight up. Floor after floor, that is a set of single-leg presses built into your day. And here is the skinny advantage: the load is your body, so a lighter body can climb more floors, more often, with less joint cost. The heavy guy takes the elevator to save his knees. You take the stairs and build yours.
Climb with me for forty five seconds. Steady pace, full foot, push the step away. Feel where the burn starts. That feeling is the whole lesson. Go.

The protocol is a rule, not a workout. If there are stairs, you take them. Every time, every day, no negotiation at the elevator door. Keep the pace steady and your hands off the rail, because the rail is a refund on the work. If your building has two floors, climb them twice. The dose looks tiny because it is spread across your whole life, and that spread is exactly why it works. Frequency beats intensity when the goal is legs that never quit.

So, your floor. Under two: the burn owns you right now, and daily stairs are the fastest way to take the building back. Two to three: ordinary legs, one month from noticeably stronger. Over three: your legs already treat gravity like a suggestion. Retest in thirty days, same staircase, same pace, and count the floors again. Put your floor in the comments. Just the number. We will see whose building got smaller.

The elevator will keep offering. Keep declining. Every floor you climb is a deposit your legs cash in as power. Subscribe, and bring me your new floor in thirty days. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: What Happens to Your leg power If You take the stairs Every Day
